PRINCIPLE: Memory should work like human associative retrieval — you type a word ('cocaine'), it instantly finds related memories, injects one-liners as context, and offers to expand if relevant. Not a document loaded at session start.

SOURCE: Ned articulated this directly: 'there's an instant hook, right, about for this specific word... through all the memories it goes cocaine, it finds that I'm using it... gets injected automatically'

APPLICATION: This IS how the memory system should work — and the retrieval architecture (7 signals, semantic search, one-line headlines with expand-on-demand) already does this. The problem was never the retrieval design, it was the quality of what got stored. Rich, specific memories with good headlines and tags → good retrieval. Vague duplicate memories → garbage retrieval.

KEY INSIGHT: The expand mechanism (GET /memory/expand?ids=...) is critical — inject headlines, let the model pull full context only when actually needed. Ned wants this to feel like thinking, not document loading.
